Dr. Varga has publicly endorsed several local public-health initiatives that the Brennick council later adopted with good results.
UV disinfection systems typically cost more to install than chlorine systems of comparable capacity.
Most Brennick residents who were surveyed could not tell the difference in taste between UV-treated and chlorinated water.
Cardiologists routinely advise their patients about the cardiovascular health risks posed by contaminants in drinking water.
questions.explanation: The argument rests entirely on a cardiologist's authority about water-treatment safety, a field outside her specialty (bad authority). A weakens it by showing that the people with the relevant expertise reach the opposite verdict. E is the tempting trap: it concerns her expertise, but it bolsters her standing on the topic and so strengthens rather than weakens. C gives a different reason to avoid UV, which does nothing to undercut the safety claim the argument relies on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brennick should not adopt UV disinfection.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dr. Varga, a renowned cardiologist devoted to human health, says UV leaves water less safe than chlorine.

breakdown.analysis: A cardiologist knows hearts, not water treatment. 'Devoted to human health' is a broad label that doesn't make her an expert in disinfection systems. It's like asking a dentist whether your roof will leak because both are about 'protecting your home.' To weaken, show that the people who actually know water treatment disagree.

choices.note: CORRECT. Water-treatment engineers, the relevant experts, say UV works at least as well as chlorine for Brennick's water. That directly contradicts the claim the argument rests on.
This makes Varga look like a good adviser, which if anything helps Ostrow. Past local successes don't show she's right about UV.
Cost is a different reason to avoid UV. The argument is about safety, and this does nothing to undercut the safety claim.
Taste isn't the issue. Safety is. Irrelevant.
Trap. This bolsters Varga's standing on drinking-water risks, which strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

questions.stimulus: Proponents of the new Kessler dance notation argue that the older Arnaud system records partnered lifts too imprecisely to serve the needs of choreographic archives. Admittedly, Kessler notation is now taught at two conservatories. But the Arnaud system has been the archival standard for over a century, and nearly every major dance company still files its scores in it. A system that so many companies have relied on for so long would hardly have survived if it recorded lifts too imprecisely for archival use. So the proponents' claim is mistaken.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about the training offered at conservatories from evidence concerning only two of them
attacks the motives of the notation's proponents rather than the evidence they offer
concludes that one notation system is superior to another in every respect on the basis of evidence about a single respect
presupposes the truth of the very claim about lifts that it sets out to establish
treats the long-standing, widespread use of a practice as proof that the practice is not deficient in a particular respect
questions.explanation: The argument rebuts a specific claim about lift notation by appealing to tradition and popularity: because the Arnaud system has long been widely used, it must not be too imprecise. E describes that inappropriate appeal in abstract terms. C is the tempting trap because it names a real-sounding scope flaw, but the conclusion concerns only the lift-recording claim, not superiority in every respect. A misreads the role of the two conservatories, which are a concession and not the basis for any generalization.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proponents' claim that Arnaud notation records lifts too imprecisely is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Arnaud has been the archival standard for over a century; nearly every major company still uses it; a system relied on so long wouldn't survive if it recorded lifts too imprecisely.

breakdown.analysis: 'Everyone has used it forever' doesn't mean it does a particular job well. Systems survive for lots of reasons: habit, switching costs, no alternative. It's like saying fax machines can't be slow because offices used them for decades. Prephrase: appeal to tradition and popularity to deny a specific weakness.

choices.note: The two conservatories are just a concession. The argument doesn't generalize from them to anything.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Two conservatories teach Kessler notation, so all conservatories must be switching to it.

choices.note: No attack on motives. The argument ignores who the proponents are entirely.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The proponents of Kessler notation sell Kessler textbooks, so their claim is self-serving.

choices.note: Trap. The conclusion is narrow: it only denies that Arnaud is too imprecise for lifts. It never claims Arnaud is better in every respect.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Arnaud records turns more precisely than Kessler, so Arnaud is superior in every way.

choices.note: Not circular. The argument offers outside evidence (long, widespread use). The evidence is just weak.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Arnaud records lifts precisely, because its lift notation is accurate.

choices.note: CORRECT. Long-standing, widespread use is treated as proof that the system isn't deficient in one specific respect (lifts). Popularity and tradition don't establish that.

questions.stimulus: Tobias Wren is the most widely respected appraiser of antique clocks in the country; collectors and auction houses accept his valuations without question, and dealers routinely quote his estimates in their catalogues. Wren has said that lubricating the fusee chain of an antique clock with modern synthetic oil slowly corrodes the chain. Therefore, restorers should avoid using synthetic oils on fusee chains.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: A clockmaker warned that a mainspring could snap if it is overwound. The mainspring in this carriage clock has been overwound. Therefore, the mainspring in this carriage clock will snap.

Imelda Rusk is the region's most sought-after auditor of credit unions; boards accept her financial findings without dispute. Rusk has said that the carpet chosen for the new branch office will wear through within five years. So the credit union should choose a different carpet.

Most members of the Fallon Hospice volunteer association, who have worked closely with patients' families for years, believe that evening visiting hours should be extended. Therefore, evening visiting hours at Fallon Hospice should be extended.

Petra Lund, a volcanologist who has monitored gas emissions at the Askar caldera for thirty years and whose forecasts are widely trusted, says that the recent changes in emissions there indicate rising magma below the caldera. Therefore, the evacuation plan for nearby villages should be reviewed.

Coach Dalby argues that the esports league's new ranking formula is unfair to young teams, but Dalby's own team, which has many young players, is ranked poorly under that formula. Therefore, the ranking formula is fair to young teams.
questions.explanation: The original cites an authority who is renowned for one competence (appraising value) as decisive on a different matter (the chemistry of lubricants and metal), then recommends action. B mirrors this exactly: an auditor's financial authority is used to settle a question about carpet durability. D is the tempting surface match, but Lund speaks within her own field, so its reasoning is not flawed in the same way. C appeals to popular opinion rather than misplaced expertise, and E is ad hominem; A treats a possibility as a certainty.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Restorers should avoid synthetic oils on fusee chains.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wren, the most respected appraiser of antique clocks, says synthetic oil slowly corrodes fusee chains.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A person is a top authority on A; they make a claim about B; so act on the claim about B.

breakdown.analysis: Wren is great at valuing clocks. Whether synthetic oil corrodes metal is a chemistry and restoration question. Being an expert on prices doesn't make you an expert on corrosion. It's like trusting a real-estate appraiser about whether your foundation has termites. Find the answer where someone's expertise in one area is used to settle a question in another.

choices.note: Different flaw: it turns 'could snap' into 'will snap.' That's treating a possibility as a certainty, not misplaced authority.
CORRECT. Rusk is a top auditor, and her financial authority is used to settle a question about carpet durability. Same structure: expertise in one field, claim in another, recommendation follows.
Different flaw: appeal to popular opinion among volunteers. And arguably they do have relevant experience with families.
Trap. It looks the same, but Lund is a volcanologist talking about volcanoes. That's appropriate authority, so the reasoning isn't flawed the same way.
Different flaw: ad hominem (Dalby has a motive), plus treating a bad argument as proof the opposite is true.

questions.stimulus: Tiltmeters on the summit of Mount Orrin have recorded steady ground inflation for six weeks, a pattern that at other volcanoes has often preceded eruptions. The regional monitoring board nonetheless left Orrin's alert level unchanged, citing the view of Dr. Kalen Mott that the readings reflect frost heave in the instrument housings rather than actual ground deformation. Dr. Mott is the world's foremost authority on the chemistry of volcanic gases. The board's decision was therefore well founded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Dr. Mott has never misjudged the significance of the monitoring data from any of the volcanoes she has studied over her long career at observatories around the world.
Frost heave is the most frequent cause of spurious tiltmeter readings at volcanoes with cold summits.
Dr. Mott has no personal or professional stake in whether the monitoring board decides to raise Orrin's alert level.
Judging whether tiltmeter readings reflect ground deformation does not require expertise that a volcanic-gas chemist would ordinarily lack.
The volcanoes at which steady inflation preceded eruptions are representative of volcanoes in general.
questions.explanation: The only support for the board's decision is Mott's authority, but her expertise is in gas chemistry while the question concerns instrument readings of ground deformation; the argument needs her expertise to be relevant (bad authority). D states that requirement in negated form: if judging tiltmeter data did require expertise she lacks, citing her would give the decision no support. C is the most tempting trap. It addresses bias, a different flaw, and while a stake might cast doubt on her, the argument does not depend on her being disinterested. A is far too strong, B would strengthen but is not required, and E concerns evidence the argument sets aside rather than relies on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board's decision to leave Orrin's alert level unchanged was well founded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Six weeks of steady inflation often precedes eruptions; Dr. Mott says the readings are frost heave; Mott is the top authority on volcanic-gas chemistry.

breakdown.analysis: The only support for the decision is Mott's say-so. But she's a gas chemist, and the question is whether tiltmeter readings reflect real ground movement. If reading tiltmeters takes expertise a gas chemist doesn't have, citing her gives the board nothing. It's like trusting a world-class cardiologist to read your knee X-ray. So the argument must assume her gas-chemistry expertise doesn't leave her unqualified to judge tiltmeter data.

choices.note: Way too strong. An expert can be reliable without a perfect career record. Negate it (she's misjudged data once) and the argument barely moves.
choices.negation: Dr. Mott has misjudged the significance of monitoring data from at least one volcano she has studied.

choices.note: Would help a bit, but isn't required. Negate it (frost heave isn't the most frequent cause) and Mott could still be right about this case.
choices.negation: Frost heave is not the most frequent cause of spurious tiltmeter readings at volcanoes with cold summits.

choices.note: Trap. It's about bias, a different issue. Negate it (she has some stake) and that might cast doubt, but having a stake doesn't make her wrong. The argument doesn't depend on her being disinterested.
choices.negation: Dr. Mott has some personal or professional stake in whether the board raises Orrin's alert level.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: judging tiltmeter readings requires expertise a gas chemist would ordinarily lack. Then Mott's authority means nothing here, and the decision has no support. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: Judging whether tiltmeter readings reflect ground deformation does require expertise that a volcanic-gas chemist would ordinarily lack.

choices.note: The argument sets the eruption pattern aside rather than relying on it. Negate it and, if anything, the inflation looks less alarming, which helps the board.
choices.negation: The volcanoes at which steady inflation preceded eruptions are not representative of volcanoes in general.

questions.stimulus: At the annual meeting of the Larchmont Teachers Credit Union, member Pavel Oduya proposed that the credit union stop charging overdraft fees. Board chair Renata Lisk urged members to reject the proposal without further discussion. Oduya, she pointed out, has paid more in overdraft fees over the past year than any other member, so he is plainly motivated by self-interest rather than by concern for the institution.
questions.stem: The argument is flawed in that it
choices: presumes that a policy benefiting some members must harm the credit union as a whole
rejects a proposal on the basis of a claim about the motives of the person who made it
treats the board chair's position as sufficient evidence that her judgment is correct
fails to consider that overdraft fees may be an important source of revenue for the credit union
generalizes from the behavior of one member to the behavior of all members
questions.explanation: Lisk never addresses the merits of eliminating overdraft fees; she dismisses the proposal by pointing to Oduya's personal interest in it, a classic ad hominem. B describes this. D is the tempting trap because it sounds like a sensible objection to the proposal, but it is a consideration that would support Lisk's conclusion, so overlooking it is not a flaw in her reasoning. C is wrong because Lisk relies on a claim about Oduya, not on her own position as chair.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Members should reject Oduya's proposal to stop charging overdraft fees, without further discussion.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Oduya paid more in overdraft fees than anyone last year, so he's motivated by self-interest.

breakdown.analysis: Lisk never says why overdraft fees are good or bad. She just points at Oduya's motive. But a self-interested person can still be right. It's like dismissing a smoker's argument for smoke detectors because he's worried about his own house. Prephrase: ad hominem, attacking the person instead of the proposal.

choices.note: Lisk never says the policy would harm the credit union. She doesn't discuss its effects at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dropping overdraft fees helps members who overdraw, so it must hurt the credit union.

choices.note: CORRECT. The proposal is rejected because of a claim about Oduya's motives, not because of anything wrong with the proposal itself.
Lisk doesn't say 'trust me because I'm chair.' She relies on a claim about Oduya.
choices.example: Example of flaw: I'm the board chair, so my view on fees is correct.

choices.note: Trap. This is a good point against the proposal, so it would support Lisk's conclusion. Leaving it out isn't what makes her reasoning flawed.
Lisk talks about one member's motives. She doesn't generalize to all members.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Oduya overdraws all the time, so most members must overdraw all the time.

questions.stimulus: Dr. Imani Royce has published research indicating that patients at the Fairhollow Hospice who received music therapy reported significantly less pain over a three-month period than comparable patients who did not. However, Dr. Royce's research was funded by the Harmonia Foundation, an organization that promotes music therapy programs. Hospice administrators should therefore disregard her findings when deciding whether to adopt music therapy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Music therapy is not effective at reducing the pain experienced by patients in hospice care.
The Harmonia Foundation funds research only by scientists who were already known to favor music therapy before applying.
The patients who received music therapy at Fairhollow were representative of hospice patients generally.
Dr. Royce's funding from the Harmonia Foundation gives some reason to doubt the accuracy of her reported findings.
No other published study has found that music therapy reduces the pain experienced by hospice patients.
questions.explanation: The argument dismisses Royce's findings solely because of who funded her, so it must assume that the funding source bears on the findings' reliability (the gap in a circumstantial ad hominem). If the funding gave no reason at all for doubt, D's negation, the argument collapses. A is the tempting trap, but the argument concludes only that the findings should be disregarded, not that music therapy is ineffective. B is far stronger than needed, C would support Royce rather than the argument, and E is not required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hospice administrators should disregard Royce's findings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Royce's research was funded by the Harmonia Foundation, which promotes music therapy.

breakdown.analysis: The only reason to toss the findings is who paid for them. For that to work, the funding has to give at least some reason to doubt the results. If it gives no reason at all, the argument has nothing left. Note how weak the assumption is: it only needs 'some reason to doubt,' not proof of fraud. It's like ignoring a car review because the automaker paid for it: that move only makes sense if the payment could plausibly skew the review.

choices.note: Trap. The conclusion is that we should disregard the findings, not that music therapy doesn't work. Negate it (music therapy does work) and the argument about ignoring this particular study still stands.
choices.negation: Music therapy is effective at reducing the pain of patients in hospice care.

choices.note: Far too strong. The argument doesn't need Harmonia to fund only pre-committed believers. Negate it and the funding could still give reason for doubt.
choices.negation: The Harmonia Foundation funds at least some research by scientists who were not already known to favor music therapy.

choices.note: This is about whether Royce's results generalize, which would support Royce, not the argument. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument.
choices.negation: The patients who received music therapy at Fairhollow were not representative of hospice patients generally.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the funding gives no reason at all to doubt the findings. Then the only reason to disregard them is gone, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: Dr. Royce's funding from the Harmonia Foundation gives no reason to doubt the accuracy of her findings.

choices.note: Not required. The argument is about whether to trust this study. Negate it (other studies agree) and the argument about Royce's funding is unaffected.
choices.negation: At least one other published study has found that music therapy reduces hospice patients' pain.

questions.stimulus: Critics of the Vantor Pro League's new anti-cheating software claim that it frequently flags legitimate players as cheaters. But nearly all of these critics are players whose own accounts the software has flagged. Players who were caught cheating obviously have every reason to discredit the system that caught them, so their complaints tell us nothing. Hence the software must rarely, if ever, flag legitimate players.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Most flagged players who appealed were reinstated after independent reviewers found no evidence that they had cheated.
Several of the critics have publicly objected to other league policies, including its rules on player transfers.
The company that developed the anti-cheating software has a financial interest in the league's continuing to use that software.
Cheating in professional esports leagues has become considerably more common over the past several years.
Few players whose accounts have never been flagged by the software have complained to the league about it.
questions.explanation: The argument dismisses the critics because they were flagged, assuming that being flagged means they were caught cheating and so have a motive to lie (ad hominem). A undercuts this: independent review cleared most appellants, so many flagged critics were legitimate players, which is exactly what the critics allege. C is the most tempting trap; it turns the same motive-based attack on the developer, but the argument does not rely on any claim by the developer, so C does not weaken it. E strengthens the argument, and B and D are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The anti-cheating software rarely, if ever, flags legitimate players.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly all critics were flagged by the software; players caught cheating have a reason to discredit it; so their complaints tell us nothing.

breakdown.analysis: The argument assumes that being flagged means being caught cheating. But that's the very question! If the software flags innocent players, then flagged critics are exactly the people who'd know. Even setting that aside, a motive to complain doesn't make the complaint false. It's like dismissing everyone who says a speed camera is broken because they all got tickets. To weaken, show that many flagged players were actually innocent.

choices.note: CORRECT. Independent reviewers cleared most flagged players who appealed. So many flagged critics were legitimate players, which is exactly what the critics claimed. The argument's dismissal falls apart.
Critics complaining about other policies doesn't tell us whether the software is accurate. Irrelevant.
Trap. It turns the same motive attack on the developer. But the argument doesn't rely on anything the developer said, so this doesn't touch it.
More cheating overall doesn't tell us whether the software wrongly flags legitimate players. If anything, it makes more flags seem deserved.
This strengthens the argument: the complaints come almost only from flagged players, which fits the 'sour grapes' story.

questions.stimulus: Engineer Tomas Brill contends that the Westmere water plant's aging filtration membranes should be replaced this year, since they now remove too few contaminants to meet the city's standards. But Brill works for the company that manufactures the replacement membranes, so of course he wants the city to buy them. Clearly, then, the membranes do not need to be replaced this year.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Each section of the Larch Valley vineyard has excellent drainage. Therefore, the vineyard as a whole has excellent drainage, and it is unlikely to suffer from root rot.

Rowena Pike, a dealer in antique clocks, contends that a rare bracket clock is worth more than its asking price. Since Pike profits from sales of such clocks, her claim should be checked by an independent appraiser before any collector agrees to buy the clock at that price.
Most of the Sarnia Esports League's fans prefer longer matches. Therefore, longer matches would be best for the league.
A seismologist warned that the Halden fault could produce a major earthquake. Therefore, a major earthquake will occur on the Halden fault.

Hospice administrator Lena Corso argues that the hospice should hire two more night nurses. But Corso's sister is a nurse who is looking for night work, so Corso clearly has a personal reason to want new hires. It follows that the hospice does not need additional night nurses.
questions.explanation: The original rejects a claim because its proponent has a personal interest in it, and then concludes that the claim is false (ad hominem). E matches both steps: Corso's personal stake is taken to show that the hospice does not need more nurses. B is the tempting trap because it also notes a speaker's financial interest, but it reasonably concludes only that her claim should be independently verified, which is not flawed. A is a part-to-whole inference, C an appeal to popularity, and D treats a possibility as a certainty.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The membranes do not need to be replaced this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brill says they should be replaced; Brill works for the company that sells replacements, so he wants the city to buy them.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Person says X; person benefits if X is accepted; so X is false.

breakdown.analysis: The argument attacks Brill's motive, and then goes further: it concludes the opposite of what he said. But a seller can be right. A mechanic who sells brake pads might still be telling the truth that your brakes are shot. Find the answer that uses a personal stake to conclude the claim is false.

choices.note: Different flaw: part to whole. Each section drains well, so the whole vineyard does.
Trap. It also notes a financial interest, but it only concludes that the claim should be checked by someone independent. That's reasonable, not flawed.
Different flaw: appeal to popularity. Fans prefer it, so it's best for the league.
Different flaw: 'could produce' becomes 'will occur.' A possibility treated as a certainty.
CORRECT. Corso has a personal reason to want new hires, so the argument concludes the hospice doesn't need them. Same two steps: point out the motive, then conclude the claim is false.

questions.stimulus: Choreographer Anouk Selten has argued that dance companies should record every new work in full notation rather than relying solely on video, on the grounds that video fails to capture a dancer's shifts of weight unambiguously. Selten's argument may sound persuasive, but it should be rejected. Of the eleven works she has created in the past decade, she has had only two fully notated; the rest exist only on video. Someone who does not follow her own recommendation cannot be taken seriously when she makes it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about all of Selten's choreographic works on the basis of a sample of only eleven of them
attributes to Selten the view that video recordings of dance have no value
takes a discrepancy between a person's recommendation and her own practice as a reason to reject the recommendation
fails to address the possibility that video recordings capture some aspects of a live performance that notation cannot
confuses the claim that full notation is sufficient for preserving a dance work with the claim that it is necessary
questions.explanation: The argument never engages Selten's reason (that video records weight shifts ambiguously); it rejects her argument because her own practice is inconsistent with it, a 'you too' form of ad hominem. C states this abstractly. D is the most tempting trap: it sounds like a weakness, but it is a consideration that would count against Selten and thus for the argument's conclusion, so failing to mention it is not what makes the reasoning flawed. B describes a straw man the argument does not commit, since it never restates Selten's view, and A and E name flaws absent from the reasoning.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Selten's argument for full notation should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only two of her eleven works are fully notated; someone who doesn't follow her own advice can't be taken seriously.

breakdown.analysis: Selten gave a reason: video doesn't capture weight shifts clearly. The argument never touches that reason. It just says she's a hypocrite. But hypocrisy doesn't make advice wrong. A smoking doctor who tells you to quit is still right. Prephrase: the argument rejects a recommendation because the person doesn't follow it.

choices.note: The argument doesn't conclude anything about all her works. It uses her eleven works to show she doesn't follow her advice, which is accurate.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Selten's last eleven works were all lighthearted, so all of her works must be lighthearted.

choices.note: The argument never says Selten thinks video is worthless. It doesn't misstate her view at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Selten thinks video is completely useless, which is absurd, so her argument fails.

choices.note: CORRECT. The gap between what Selten recommends and what she does is used as a reason to reject the recommendation. That's the 'you too' flaw.
Trap. This would be a point against Selten, so it supports the argument's conclusion. Not mentioning it isn't the flaw.
The argument doesn't discuss whether notation is necessary or sufficient for preservation. No conditional confusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Notation is enough to preserve a dance, so any dance without notation will be lost.

questions.stimulus: Researchers have found that the Dorrel leaf beetle, which was recently discovered in a vineyard just across the county line, is capable of carrying Kestine blight, a bacterial disease that kills grapevines. The beetle can fly several kilometers in a single season. Therefore, unless the vineyards of Allard County begin spraying for the beetle immediately, their vines will be killed by Kestine blight.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on findings from researchers who may have a financial interest in the sale of the pesticides used against the beetle
assumes that a disease capable of killing grapevines will also harm the other crops grown in Allard County
generalizes from a single vineyard to all vineyards in the state
treats the mere possibility that the beetle will spread the blight to the county's vines as though it were certain
fails to consider that spraying for the beetle might also kill insects that protect the county's vines from other pests
questions.explanation: The premises establish only that the beetle can carry the blight and has been found nearby; the conclusion asserts that, without spraying, the vines will be killed. D identifies this jump from possibility to certainty. E is the tempting trap because it is a reasonable concern about spraying, but the argument makes no claim about spraying's side effects, so ignoring them does not weaken its inference. A speculates about motives the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless Allard County vineyards spray for the beetle immediately, their vines will be killed by Kestine blight.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Dorrel beetle can carry the blight; it was found just across the county line; it can fly several kilometers a season.

breakdown.analysis: 'Can carry' and 'is nearby' make the blight possible. The conclusion says the vines will be killed. That's a leap from could to will. Maybe these beetles don't carry the blight, maybe they won't fly this way, maybe the vines survive. It's like hearing a coworker has a cold and declaring you'll definitely be sick next week. You can't pick a conclusion on a possibility.

choices.note: The passage never mentions who funded the researchers or any pesticide sales. Pure speculation.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The beetle researchers work for a pesticide company, so their findings about the beetle can't be trusted.

choices.note: The argument only talks about grapevines. It never says anything about other crops.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The blight kills grapevines, so it will wipe out the county's apple orchards too.

choices.note: No sampling. The argument isn't drawing conclusions about all vineyards in the state from one vineyard.
choices.example: Example of flaw: One vineyard near the border found the beetle, so every vineyard in the state is infested.

choices.note: CORRECT. The premises show the beetle could bring the blight. The conclusion says the vines will be killed. Possibility treated as certainty.
Trap. A sensible worry about spraying, but the argument makes no claim about spraying's side effects. Ignoring them doesn't break its inference about the blight.

questions.stimulus: Member of the Pinecrest Credit Union: Our board plans to approve a merger with Halden Savings, and members should oppose it. Under the merger terms, the combined institution would be permitted, though not required, to close any branch whose annual transaction volume falls below a set threshold. Our Elm Street branch has fallen below that threshold in two of the last five years. So if the merger goes through, the Elm Street branch will be closed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Several other Pinecrest branches have also fallen below the transaction threshold in recent years.
Members who use the Elm Street branch are, on average, older than members who use Pinecrest's other branches.
The merger terms would allow the combined institution to close branches below the threshold but would not require it to close them.
Closing a branch generally reduces a financial institution's operating costs.
In its previous mergers, Halden Savings agreed to identical closure terms but closed none of the branches that became eligible.
questions.explanation: The argument treats permission to close a branch as a guarantee that it will be closed (possibility taken as certainty). E weakens it by showing that, under identical terms, Halden has not actually closed eligible branches, making closure less likely. C is the tempting trap: it points at the gap but merely restates what the premise already says ('permitted, though not required'), adding no reason to think closure is unlikely. D, if anything, supplies a motive for closure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the merger goes through, the Elm Street branch will be closed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The combined institution would be permitted, not required, to close branches below a volume threshold; Elm Street fell below it in two of the last five years.

breakdown.analysis: Permission isn't a decision. 'Allowed to close' doesn't mean 'will close.' Notice too that Elm Street was below the threshold in only two of five years, so it might not even qualify. It's like saying your landlord will evict you because the lease lets him end it with 30 days' notice. To weaken, give a reason to think closure is unlikely even with permission.

choices.note: Other branches being eligible doesn't make Elm Street's closure less likely. If anything it suggests many branches are at risk.
The age of Elm Street's customers doesn't tell us whether the branch would be closed. Irrelevant.
Trap. It points right at the gap, but it just repeats the premise ('permitted, though not required'). It adds no reason to think closure won't happen.
This gives a motive to close branches, which if anything strengthens the argument.
CORRECT. Halden has agreed to the same terms before and closed none of the eligible branches. That's real evidence the permission won't be used, so closure becomes unlikely.

questions.stimulus: Geologists are confident that Mount Tavel will erupt at some point in the next century. Even small amounts of volcanic ash can damage jet engines. An eruption of Mount Tavel could send enough ash across the Serin Valley to force the valley's airport to close. Thus the Serin Valley airport will be closed by volcanic ash at some point in the next century.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The Linden Ballet will adopt Kessler notation next season. Adopting a new notation system could slow a company's rehearsals. Thus the Linden Ballet's rehearsals might be slowed next season.

The Rowan Hospice will certainly expand its nursing staff next year. Expanding a nursing staff could produce scheduling conflicts among nurses. Thus the Rowan Hospice will experience scheduling conflicts among its nurses next year.

Whenever the Kellan reservoir drops below its minimum level, the water plant must switch to its backup supply. The reservoir will drop below its minimum level this summer. Thus the plant will switch to its backup supply this summer.
Most esports teams that change coaches in midseason fail to make the playoffs. Thus changing coaches in midseason causes teams to miss the playoffs.
Each gear in this clock movement was cut by a master craftsman. Thus the movement as a whole is a masterpiece of craftsmanship.
questions.explanation: The original moves from a certain event and a consequence that event could have to the claim that the consequence will occur (possibility treated as certainty). B has the same structure: a certain staff expansion plus a possible effect yields 'will experience conflicts.' A is the tempting trap because its structure is nearly identical, but its conclusion says only that rehearsals 'might' be slowed, which follows; it is not flawed. C is a valid conditional argument, D infers causation from correlation, and E reasons from parts to whole.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Serin Valley airport will be closed by volcanic ash at some point in the next century.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mount Tavel will almost certainly erupt in the next century; ash damages jet engines; an eruption could send enough ash to close the airport.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A will happen; A could cause B; so B will happen.

breakdown.analysis: The eruption is certain, but closing the airport is only something an eruption could do. 'Could' turns into 'will' in the conclusion. It's like saying: I'm definitely driving to work tomorrow, driving could get me a flat tire, so I'll get a flat tire tomorrow. Find the answer with a certain event, a possible effect, and a 'will' conclusion.

choices.note: Trap: same structure up to the end, but the conclusion says rehearsals 'might' be slowed. That follows from the premises, so it isn't flawed.
CORRECT. The expansion is certain, and it could cause scheduling conflicts. The conclusion says conflicts will happen. Same could-to-will jump.
Valid conditional argument: below minimum → switch; it will drop below; so it will switch. No flaw.
Different flaw: correlation treated as causation.
Different flaw: part to whole. Masterful gears don't guarantee a masterful movement.

questions.stimulus: The Corvel water authority plans to replace chlorine disinfection with a new ozone system. Opponents point out that ozone treatment can, under certain conditions, produce bromate, a compound that is regulated as a drinking-water contaminant. Since Corvel's source water contains bromide, the substance from which bromate forms, the opponents conclude that switching to ozone will cause Corvel's drinking water to exceed the legal limit for bromate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Ozone treatment produces bromate in excess of the legal limit whenever the water it treats contains any bromide at all.
Chlorine disinfection does not produce any compounds that are regulated as drinking-water contaminants.
Corvel's source water does not contain so little bromide that ozone treatment could not push bromate above the legal limit.
The opponents of the ozone system have no financial ties to suppliers of chlorine.
Most of the water systems that have switched from chlorine to ozone have subsequently exceeded the legal limit for bromate.
questions.explanation: The opponents move from 'ozone can produce bromate under certain conditions' and 'Corvel's water contains some bromide' to the certainty that the legal limit will be exceeded. At a minimum they must assume that Corvel's bromide level is not too low for an exceedance even to be possible; negate C and the conclusion cannot hold. A is the most tempting trap, but it is stronger than needed and still would not guarantee exceeding the limit, so the argument does not depend on it. D raises bias, a different flaw the argument never invokes, and B and E are not required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching to ozone will cause Corvel's water to exceed the legal limit for bromate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ozone can, under certain conditions, produce bromate; Corvel's source water contains bromide, which bromate forms from.

breakdown.analysis: The opponents leap from 'can produce bromate under some conditions' to 'will exceed the legal limit.' That's a big jump. A necessary assumption is the minimum the argument needs, and the bare minimum here is that exceeding the limit is even possible: Corvel's water can't have so little bromide that ozone couldn't push bromate over the limit. If it did, the conclusion would be impossible. It's like predicting you'll get a sunburn when it's barely bright out: you at least need enough sun for a burn to happen.

choices.note: Trap. This would help the argument a lot, but it's much stronger than needed. Negate it (some bromide levels don't produce excess bromate) and Corvel's level could still be high enough. The argument doesn't depend on it.
choices.negation: Ozone treatment does not produce excess bromate in at least some water that contains bromide.

choices.note: Not needed. The argument is about whether ozone will exceed the bromate limit, not about comparing with chlorine. Negating it (chlorine also produces regulated compounds) doesn't touch the conclusion.
choices.negation: Chlorine disinfection produces at least one compound regulated as a drinking-water contaminant.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: Corvel's water has so little bromide that ozone couldn't push bromate over the limit. Then the conclusion is impossible. The argument needs this.
choices.negation: Corvel's source water contains so little bromide that ozone treatment could not push bromate above the legal limit.

choices.note: The opponents' financial ties don't affect whether the reasoning works. Negating it changes nothing about the argument's logic.
choices.negation: At least one opponent of the ozone system has financial ties to chlorine suppliers.

choices.note: Not required. Other systems' records might help, but the argument is about Corvel's water. Negate it (most switchers didn't exceed) and the argument could still be true for Corvel.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the water systems that switched to ozone have exceeded the bromate limit.

questions.stimulus: Conservator: The dial of this longcase clock, attributed to the eighteenth-century maker Josiah Pell, uses only pigments that were available in Pell's era, and the gearing of its movement matches a design Pell is known to have used. Admittedly, other makers of that period used the same pigments, and Pell's gearing design was widely copied. Still, these findings show that the clock could well have come from Pell's workshop. So the clock is a genuine Pell and should be catalogued as such.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: moves from evidence establishing only that a claim might be true to the conclusion that the claim is true
relies on the testimony of a source concerning a matter that lies outside that source's field of expertise
generalizes from the features of a single clock to all clocks attributed to the same maker
uses its acknowledgment of a counterconsideration as though that acknowledgment provided support for its conclusion
presupposes in its premises that the clock was made in Pell's workshop
questions.explanation: The conservator's own intermediate conclusion is that the clock 'could well' be Pell's, yet she concludes that it is a genuine Pell; that is a shift from possibility to certainty, as A states. D is the most tempting trap: the concession does undercut the evidence, but the argument does not use it as support, it sets it aside with 'Still.' E names a circular flaw that is not present, since matching a known Pell design does not presuppose Pell's authorship. B and C describe bad-authority and sampling flaws the argument does not commit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The clock is a genuine Pell and should be catalogued as such.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The dial uses only pigments available in Pell's era; the gearing matches a Pell design; but other makers used those pigments and Pell's design was widely copied; so the clock could well be Pell's.

breakdown.analysis: The conservator says it herself: the evidence shows the clock 'could well' be Pell's. Then she concludes it is Pell's. That's possible jumping to certain. The concession actually makes it worse: the evidence fits lots of makers. It's like saying a suspect could have done it because he was in town, and then announcing he's guilty.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence establishes only that the clock might be Pell's (her own words: 'could well'). The conclusion says it is Pell's.
No outside source is cited at all. The conservator is reasoning from physical evidence in her own field.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous clock collector, who is a lawyer by training, says the pigments are authentic, so they are.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about this one clock. No generalization to all Pell clocks.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This Pell clock uses period pigments, so all clocks attributed to Pell do.

choices.note: Trap. The concession does undercut the evidence, but the argument doesn't use it as support. It sets it aside with 'Still.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: Admittedly, many makers copied Pell's design. That just shows how important Pell was, so this clock must be his.

choices.note: Not circular. Matching a known Pell design doesn't assume the clock is a Pell; it's evidence for it, just weak evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This clock is a genuine Pell, because it was made in Pell's workshop.

questions.stimulus: The Corran Esports League ranks individual players on the basis of their performance in league matches over the past two seasons. Each of the five players on the Ironvale Wolves currently ranks among the league's top twenty individual players, and two of them rank in the top five. So the Ironvale Wolves must be one of the strongest teams in the league.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on rankings that may have been compiled by biased observers
treats rankings from one league as though they applied to another league
confuses a condition necessary for a team's success with a condition sufficient for it
fails to consider that other teams in the league might also have players who rank among the league's top twenty
presumes that a team composed of individually excellent players must itself be an excellent team
questions.explanation: The argument attributes a property of the parts (individual excellence) to the whole (the team), ignoring factors such as coordination; this is composition, as E says. D is the tempting trap, but even if other teams have strong players, that would not show the Wolves are not among the strongest; the core problem is the inference from individuals to the team. C names a different, real-sounding flaw, but the argument states no necessary condition that it then treats as sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ironvale Wolves must be one of the strongest teams in the league.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All five Wolves players rank in the top twenty individually; two rank in the top five.

breakdown.analysis: Great individual players don't guarantee a great team. Teams win through coordination, strategy, and roles fitting together. Think of an all-star team of five point guards who all want the ball. Prephrase: the argument moves from the parts (players) to the whole (team).

choices.note: Nothing suggests bias. The rankings are based on match performance, and the argument's problem is how it uses them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The rankings were compiled by a commentator who loves the Wolves, yet the argument treats them as objective.

choices.note: Only one league is involved. The rankings and the conclusion are both about the Corran league.
choices.example: Example of flaw: These players are top twenty in the amateur league, so they're top twenty in the pro league too.

choices.note: Sounds plausible, but the argument states no necessary condition that it then treats as sufficient. Its error is the part-to-whole move.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A strong team needs skilled players. The Wolves have skilled players, so they must be a strong team.

choices.note: Trap. Other teams having top players wouldn't show the Wolves aren't among the strongest. The core issue is assuming individual skill adds up to team strength.
CORRECT. The argument assumes a team of individually excellent players must be an excellent team. That's a composition flaw: what's true of the parts isn't necessarily true of the whole.

questions.stimulus: The Calloway Regional Hospice network received the highest family-satisfaction score of any hospice network in the state last year, eight points above the state average. The score was based on surveys completed by more than three thousand families. Therefore, families of patients who stayed at Brierwood House, one of the network's eleven facilities, were very likely highly satisfied with the care their relatives received.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Brierwood House is the newest of the network's eleven facilities.
The survey response rate among families at Brierwood House was similar to the response rates at the network's other ten facilities.
Family-satisfaction scores at each of the network's facilities differed only slightly from the network's overall score.
Families' satisfaction with hospice care is closely correlated with the number of nurses per patient.
Several other hospice networks in the state received scores only slightly lower than Calloway's.
questions.explanation: The argument infers that a property of the whole network (a high overall score) holds of one of its parts, a division inference that fails if facility scores vary widely. C closes that gap by showing the facilities' scores cluster tightly around the network's score. B is the tempting trap: similar response rates make the survey comparable across facilities, but they say nothing about whether Brierwood's actual score was high. E compares the network with other networks and does not address Brierwood at all.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Families at Brierwood House were very likely highly satisfied with their relatives' care.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Calloway network had the state's highest family-satisfaction score, eight points above average, based on 3,000+ surveys; Brierwood is one of the network's eleven facilities.

breakdown.analysis: A high score for the whole network doesn't tell you every facility scored high. Ten great facilities could carry one bad one. It's like saying every student at a top-ranked school must be a top student. To strengthen, show the facilities' scores don't vary much, so the network's score really reflects each one.

choices.note: Being newest tells us nothing about satisfaction. Irrelevant.
Trap. Similar response rates make the survey comparable across facilities, but they say nothing about whether Brierwood's actual score was high.
CORRECT. If every facility's score was close to the network's high score, then Brierwood's was too. That closes the gap between the whole and the part.
A general link between satisfaction and staffing doesn't tell us anything about Brierwood's staffing or its score.
This compares Calloway with other networks. It says nothing about Brierwood specifically.

questions.stimulus: Dance archivist: Every individual symbol in the Velde notation system can be learned by a novice in well under an hour, and none of the symbols requires any prior training in music or dance. Admittedly, the system contains several hundred symbols, and complete scores combine them in intricate ways. Even so, it follows that the Velde system as a whole is easy for novices to master.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: generalizes from the experiences of a small group of novice dancers to the experiences of all novices
confuses the absolute number of symbols in the system with the proportion of those symbols that are difficult to learn
relies on the judgment of an archivist about a question of teaching that lies outside her area of expertise
infers that a whole has a certain property merely because each of its parts, taken individually, has that property
treats the absence of evidence that any symbol is difficult for novices to learn as proof that none of them is
questions.explanation: From the ease of learning each symbol taken singly, the archivist concludes that the whole system is easy to master, even while conceding that there are hundreds of symbols combined intricately; this is composition, as D says. E is a tempting trap naming a different flaw, but the argument offers a positive premise that every symbol is quickly learnable rather than relying on a lack of contrary evidence. B is tempting because numbers appear, but the argument never draws an inference from a proportion. A and C describe sampling and bad-authority flaws the argument does not commit.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Velde notation system as a whole is easy for novices to master.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each symbol can be learned in under an hour with no prior training; admittedly there are hundreds of symbols combined in intricate ways.

breakdown.analysis: Each symbol is easy. But there are hundreds, combined intricately. Easy parts don't make an easy whole. Each chess piece's move takes a minute to learn, and chess is still hard to master. Prephrase: part-to-whole (composition).

choices.note: No sample of novice dancers is mentioned. The argument isn't generalizing from a group's experience.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Five novices in our workshop learned Velde quickly, so all novices will.

choices.note: Trap because numbers show up, but the argument never infers anything from a proportion. It infers from the ease of each part.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Only 20 Velde symbols are hard, fewer than in other systems, so Velde has a smaller share of hard symbols.

choices.note: The archivist isn't citing anyone's authority, and dance notation is plausibly her field. Not the flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A famous dance archivist says Velde is the easiest system to teach, so teachers should adopt it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Each symbol is easy on its own, so the archivist concludes the whole system is easy. That ignores the sheer number and the intricate combinations she herself admits.
Trap naming a different flaw. The argument has a positive premise (every symbol is quickly learnable), not just a lack of evidence that any symbol is hard.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has shown that any Velde symbol is hard, so none of them is.

questions.stimulus: Each of three biological control agents (a parasitic wasp, a predatory mite, and a fungal spray) has been shown in field trials to reduce mealybug populations in vineyards without harming the vines. The Sarno Vineyard therefore plans to release all three agents at once, expecting the combination to reduce its mealybug population more than any one of the agents would on its own.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The predatory mite readily feeds on the larvae of the parasitic wasp, and the fungal spray is lethal to the mite.
The field trials were all conducted in vineyards whose climate is considerably warmer than that of the Sarno Vineyard.
Mealybugs can transmit a virus that reduces the sugar content of grapes.
Releasing all three agents costs the vineyard considerably more than releasing any one of them would.
In the field trials, the fungal spray reduced mealybug populations more than either of the other two agents did.
questions.explanation: The plan assumes that because each agent works individually, the combination will work at least as well as any one of them, overlooking interactions among the parts (part-whole). A shows that the agents interfere with one another, so the combination could perform worse than one agent alone. B is the tempting trap, a representativeness worry, but a cooler climate would affect all of the agents, so it gives no reason to think the combination would underperform a single agent; it does not touch the comparative prediction. D concerns cost, not effectiveness.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Releasing all three agents at once will reduce mealybugs more than any one agent alone.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each agent (a wasp, a mite, a fungal spray) individually reduced mealybugs in field trials without harming vines.

breakdown.analysis: Each one works alone, but that doesn't mean they work together. They might interfere with each other. It's like assuming three great babysitters at once will be better than one, when they might spend the night arguing. To weaken, show the agents undercut one another.

choices.note: CORRECT. The mite eats the wasp's larvae and the spray kills the mite. Combined, the agents cancel each other out, so the combination could do worse than one agent alone.
Trap. A cooler climate might weaken all the agents, but that doesn't make the combination worse than a single agent. It doesn't touch the comparison.
This is about why mealybugs matter. It says nothing about whether the combination beats one agent.
Cost isn't the issue. The prediction is about effectiveness.
The spray being the best single agent doesn't show the combination would do worse than it. Doesn't weaken.

questions.stimulus: The Tarrow Credit Union's loan portfolio, taken as a whole, carries a lower risk of default than the portfolio of any other lender in the region, a record that Tarrow's managers attribute to its long-standing lending standards. Therefore, the mortgage that Tarrow recently issued to the Delacroix family carries a lower risk of default than most mortgages issued by other lenders in the region.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every musician in the Fennick String Quartet has won a major international competition. Therefore, the Fennick String Quartet is among the finest string quartets performing today.

The Halberd volcano-monitoring network, taken as a whole, detects tremors more reliably than any other network in the country. Therefore, the seismometer the network recently installed on Mount Esk detects tremors more reliably than most seismometers in other networks.

Every bottle in this shipment came from the Corran winery, and all of the wines that the Corran winery produces are aged in oak barrels for at least a year. Therefore, the bottle on the top shelf, which came from this shipment last week, contains wine that was aged in oak.

The average length of a patient's stay at the Linwood Hospice is shorter than the average stay at any other hospice in the county. Therefore, the Linwood Hospice admits fewer patients each year than does any other hospice in the county.

Restorers agree that the repaired regulator in this antique bracket clock could keep accurate time for at least a decade without adjustment. Therefore, the clock will keep accurate time for the next decade.
questions.explanation: The original attributes a property of a whole (the portfolio's low overall risk) to one of its parts (a particular mortgage), the division form of the part-whole flaw. B does the same, moving from the network's overall reliability to that of one seismometer. A is the most tempting trap because it is also a part-whole flaw, but it runs in the opposite direction (parts to whole, composition). C shares B's surface shape but is valid, because the property is stated to hold of every member. D confuses averages with totals, and E treats a possibility as a certainty.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Delacroix mortgage has a lower default risk than most mortgages from other regional lenders.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tarrow's portfolio as a whole has a lower default risk than any other regional lender's.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: The whole has property P better than other wholes; so one particular part has P better than most parts of other wholes.

breakdown.analysis: A low-risk portfolio can still contain a risky loan. The whole's average doesn't tell you about any one piece. It's like saying a particular player must be great because his team has the best record. Find the answer that moves from a whole's property down to one specific part (division).

choices.note: Trap: also a part-whole flaw, but backwards. It goes from parts (each musician) to the whole (the quartet). That's composition, not division.
CORRECT. The network as a whole detects tremors best, so one particular seismometer must detect them better than most others. Same move from whole to one part.
Valid. The property is stated to hold of every Corran wine, so it holds of this bottle. No flaw.
Different flaw: confuses average stay length with total admissions.
Different flaw: 'could keep accurate time' becomes 'will keep accurate time.' Possibility treated as certainty.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Lack of Evidence, Sampling, Analogy, Overreaching

questions.stimulus: Last summer, ecologists surveying the Harrow Fells searched for the crustose lichen Lecanora ferrisii, which a botanical survey recorded there in large numbers forty years ago. The survey teams examined more than two hundred boulders scattered across the fells' lower and middle slopes and found no trace of the lichen anywhere. Since the species went undetected despite so extensive a search, the ecologists concluded that it must now be extinct in the Harrow Fells.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Several other lichen species recorded in the Harrow Fells forty years ago were also absent from last summer's survey.
Air pollution, which harms many species of crustose lichen, rose sharply in the region surrounding the Harrow Fells during the 1990s and has remained high since.
Lecanora ferrisii grows almost exclusively on the faces of high cliffs, which the survey teams did not examine because of safety restrictions.
Lecanora ferrisii has recently been found in abundance in the Corran Hills, a range that lies about thirty kilometers from the Harrow Fells.
The ecologists who led last summer's survey had previously conducted similar lichen surveys in several other upland regions.
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the ecologists treat a failure to find the lichen as proof that it is gone. C shows that the search never covered the habitat where the lichen would actually be, so not finding it there says little about whether it survives in the fells. D is the tempting trap, but the conclusion concerns only the Harrow Fells; the lichen's presence in another range does nothing to show it persists there. B and E, if anything, support the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lecanora ferrisii must now be extinct in the Harrow Fells.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A survey forty years ago found it in large numbers; last summer's teams searched 200+ boulders on the lower and middle slopes and found none.

breakdown.analysis: Not finding something isn't proof it's gone, especially if you didn't look where it lives. The search covered boulders on the lower and middle slopes. What if the lichen lives somewhere else? It's like searching your living room for your keys and concluding they've been stolen, when they're in your coat pocket. To weaken, show the search missed the lichen's habitat.

choices.note: Other lichens also missing fits the idea that something wiped them out. If anything, this supports the conclusion.
This gives a reason the lichen might have died off. It strengthens the conclusion.
CORRECT. The lichen lives almost only on high cliff faces, which the teams never examined. So not finding it on boulders says almost nothing about whether it's still there.
Trap. The conclusion is only about the Harrow Fells. Finding it thirty kilometers away doesn't show it survives in the fells.
The ecologists' experience makes the survey look more credible. If anything, it helps the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Critics of the Westbury small-claims court allege that its magistrates favor landlords over tenants in disputes about security deposits. But the court's oversight board recently reviewed every complaint of bias filed against Westbury magistrates over the past five years, and it found that none of those complaints contained documentation sufficient to establish that the magistrate involved had been biased. Therefore, the magistrates of the Westbury court do not favor landlords over tenants.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats the failure of the complaints to establish that bias exists as proof that no bias exists
attacks the motives of the court's critics rather than addressing the substance of their allegation
relies on the findings of a board whose members might be unfamiliar with landlord-tenant law
presumes without justification that tenants file more complaints of bias than landlords do
infers from the fact that some magistrates are unbiased that all of the magistrates are unbiased
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: complaints that lacked enough documentation to prove bias do not show that the magistrates are unbiased, yet the argument treats them as if they did. A describes exactly this. C is the most tempting trap, but the argument's problem would remain even if the board were expert, because its finding was only that bias was not established. B describes an attack the argument never makes, and E describes a premise the argument does not contain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Westbury magistrates do not favor landlords over tenants.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The oversight board reviewed every bias complaint from the past five years and found none with documentation sufficient to establish bias.

breakdown.analysis: 'Not proven' isn't 'disproven.' Complaints lacking enough documentation just means bias wasn't established. Bias could still exist; it's often hard to document. It's like a jury acquittal being treated as proof the defendant was in another country that night. Prephrase: absence of proof treated as proof of absence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The complaints failed to establish bias, and the argument treats that as proof there is no bias. Lack of evidence isn't evidence of the opposite.
The argument doesn't say anything about the critics' motives. No ad hominem.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics are mostly tenants who lost their cases, so of course they cry bias.

choices.note: Trap. Even an expert board can only find that bias wasn't proven. The flaw remains no matter how qualified the board is.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A board of accountants reviewed the legal rulings and found them sound, so they must be sound.

choices.note: The argument never compares how often tenants and landlords complain.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most bias complaints come from tenants, so tenants must be treated worse.

choices.note: The argument doesn't start from 'some magistrates are unbiased.' It starts from complaints failing to prove bias.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Magistrate Ruiz is clearly fair, so all Westbury magistrates are fair.

questions.stimulus: Some historians have argued that the photographer Oda Marlin staged several of her celebrated street scenes, posing friends as passersby. Yet no letter, diary entry, or eyewitness account describing any such staging has ever come to light. We can therefore conclude that Marlin did not stage any of her street scenes, and that her photographs are faithful records of the moments they appear to capture.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The cargo manifest of the schooner Annick, which by law listed every item the ship carried, contains no mention of rifles. So the Annick was not carrying rifles as cargo on that voyage.

Several historians believe the mapmaker Ilse Dorn copied her coastal charts from earlier naval surveys of the northern coast. Since these historians are the leading experts on the period, Dorn must have copied her charts.
A survey of members of the Ardent Rowing Club found that they report greater well-being than most adults. So rowing must be what gives the club's members their greater sense of well-being.

Some residents claim that the Varo Company dumped solvent into Mill Creek. But inspectors who examined the company's records found nothing indicating any such dumping. So the company never dumped solvent there.
The novelist Rena Hall insists that her latest book owes nothing to earlier works. But Hall would profit from readers' believing that claim, so the book must in fact draw heavily on earlier works.
questions.explanation: The argument commits the absence-of-evidence flaw: because no record of staging has surfaced, it concludes that no staging occurred, though staging is just the sort of thing that might go unrecorded. D matches: records that would not necessarily mention illegal dumping are taken to prove there was none. A is the most tempting trap, but its inference is sound, since a manifest that by law lists every item is exactly where rifle cargo would appear. B (appeal to authority), C (correlation taken as causation), and E (attack on the source's motives) commit different flaws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Marlin did not stage any of her street scenes; her photos are faithful records.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No letter, diary, or eyewitness account describing staging has ever surfaced.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: No record of X has turned up (where X wouldn't necessarily be recorded); so X never happened.

breakdown.analysis: Staging a photo with friends is exactly the kind of thing nobody writes down. So the lack of records proves very little. It's like saying your roommate never ate your leftovers because there's no note admitting it. Find the answer that concludes 'never happened' from silence in records that wouldn't necessarily mention it.

choices.note: Trap. Looks the same, but here the manifest is legally required to list every item. If rifles were cargo, they'd be on it. So the silence is meaningful, and the reasoning is sound.
Different flaw: appeal to authority. The experts say so, so it's true.
Different flaw: correlation treated as causation. Rowers feel better, so rowing causes it.
CORRECT. The company's own records show nothing about dumping, so it never dumped. But illegal dumping is the last thing a company would record. Same leap from silence to 'never happened.'
Different flaw: an attack on the source's motive, used to conclude the opposite of her claim.

questions.stimulus: Breeders in the Kestle Valley have long claimed that some local honeybee colonies carry hyg-3, an allele that confers partial resistance to varroa mites. To test the claim, geneticists collected a total of 600 drones, drawn from every apiary in the valley, and screened tissue from each drone using the standard hyg-3 assay. None of the samples tested positive. The geneticists therefore concluded that the breeders' claim is false: no honeybee colony in the Kestle Valley carries hyg-3.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: No honeybee colony anywhere outside the Kestle Valley carries the hyg-3 allele.
The standard hyg-3 assay does not routinely fail to detect the allele in tissue that contains it.
The breeders who claimed that local colonies carry hyg-3 had no financial motive for doing so.
Any varroa resistance found in Kestle Valley colonies is not due to an allele other than hyg-3.
Every honeybee colony in the Kestle Valley contributed at least one drone to the geneticists' sample.
questions.explanation: The geneticists infer that the allele is absent because their screening did not find it, which works only if the screening could have found it. Negate B: if the assay routinely misses hyg-3 in tissue that contains it, the negative results say nothing about whether the allele is present, and the argument collapses. E is the most tempting trap, but it is too strong; a representative sample can support the conclusion without including every colony. C raises a question about motive that the geneticists' argument never relies on, and D concerns resistance rather than the allele itself.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No honeybee colony in the Kestle Valley carries hyg-3.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Geneticists screened 600 drones from every apiary in the valley with the standard hyg-3 assay; none tested positive.

breakdown.analysis: A negative test only means something if the test would have caught the allele. If the assay routinely misses hyg-3, 600 negatives tell you nothing. It's like a smoke detector with a dead battery: silence doesn't mean there's no fire. So the argument must assume the assay doesn't routinely fail to detect hyg-3.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about the Kestle Valley. Colonies elsewhere don't matter. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: At least one honeybee colony outside the Kestle Valley carries hyg-3.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the assay routinely misses hyg-3 even when it's there. Then the negative results are worthless, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: The standard hyg-3 assay routinely fails to detect the allele in tissue that contains it.

choices.note: The breeders' motives have nothing to do with whether the geneticists' test supports their conclusion. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The breeders who claimed local colonies carry hyg-3 had a financial motive for doing so.

choices.note: This is about varroa resistance, not the allele. The conclusion is only about hyg-3. Negate it (resistance comes from another allele) and the argument is untouched; if anything it fits.
choices.negation: Some varroa resistance in Kestle Valley colonies is due to an allele other than hyg-3.

choices.note: Trap. Too strong. A large sample from every apiary can support the conclusion without hitting every single colony. Negating it (one colony missed) weakens a bit but doesn't collapse the argument.
choices.negation: At least one honeybee colony in the Kestle Valley contributed no drone to the sample.

questions.stimulus: Opponents of the proposed Garrow Point desalination plant argue that its brine discharge would raise salinity at the bay's seagrass beds above the level known to damage seagrass. Admittedly, brine discharge has damaged seagrass near some other plants. But an independent two-year review modeled the Garrow Point discharge plume and was unable to establish that salinity at any seagrass bed would rise above that level. So the opponents' concern is unfounded: the plant's discharge will not push salinity at any of the bay's seagrass beds past the damaging level.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on a review that may have been influenced by parties who stand to benefit financially from the plant's approval
generalizes from damage observed at some other plants to a conclusion about the Garrow Point plant
takes for granted that damage to seagrass is the only environmental harm a desalination plant could cause
confuses a level of salinity sufficient for seagrass damage with a level necessary for such damage
treats a failure to demonstrate that a predicted outcome will occur as a demonstration that it will not occur
questions.explanation: Absence of evidence: the review could not establish that salinity would exceed the threshold, but that is not the same as showing that it will not. The model may simply have been inconclusive. E states this abstractly. A is the tempting trap because it names a familiar flaw, but the review is described as independent and the argument's problem would remain even if it were neutral. B describes a generalization the argument concedes and sets aside rather than makes, C misreads a conclusion that concerns only salinity at the seagrass beds, and D invents a conditional confusion the argument never relies on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The plant's discharge will not push salinity at any seagrass bed past the damaging level.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: An independent two-year review modeled the plume and was unable to establish that salinity at any bed would exceed that level.

breakdown.analysis: 'Couldn't show it will happen' isn't 'showed it won't happen.' The model might have been inconclusive. It's like a weather forecaster saying 'I can't confirm it'll rain,' and you leaving the umbrella home because it definitely won't. Prephrase: failure to prove X treated as proof of not-X.

choices.note: Trap. A familiar flaw, but the review is described as independent. And even a perfectly neutral review that only fails to establish the outcome still wouldn't prove the conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The plant's developer paid for the review, and the argument relies on it without question.

choices.note: The argument concedes the damage at other plants and sets it aside. It doesn't generalize from them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Brine discharge damaged seagrass at two other plants, so it will damage seagrass at Garrow Point.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about salinity at seagrass beds. It doesn't claim seagrass damage is the only possible harm.
