choices.example: Example of flaw: The plant won't hurt seagrass, so it won't harm the environment at all.

choices.note: The argument just uses one threshold level. It never mixes up sufficient and necessary conditions.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Salinity above level X damages seagrass. This seagrass is damaged, so salinity must be above X.

choices.note: CORRECT. The review failed to show salinity would cross the threshold. The argument treats that as showing it won't. Absence of proof isn't proof of absence.

questions.stimulus: To learn whether parents approve of its new animated series Pip and the Lantern, the Brightwave network posted a poll on the show's official fan website asking visitors whether they considered the program suitable for young children. Of the 2,400 parents who responded, 91 percent said that they did. Clearly, then, the vast majority of parents nationwide regard Pip and the Lantern as suitable for young children.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that some of the parents who responded may not have young children of their own
draws a conclusion about parents in general from parents likely to favor the program more than most parents do
confuses the percentage of respondents who approved of the program with the number of parents who approved of it
presumes without justification that the network conducted its poll in a deliberately misleading manner
relies on a sample far too small to support any conclusion about the views of parents across the nation
questions.explanation: Sampling: the respondents were parents visiting the show's own fan website, a group likely to be fonder of the program than parents generally. B identifies this self-selection. E is the tempting trap, but 2,400 respondents is not too small in itself; the problem is who they were, not how many. C names a percentage-versus-number confusion the argument does not make, since its conclusion is itself about proportions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The vast majority of parents nationwide think Pip and the Lantern is suitable for young children.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On the show's official fan website, 91 percent of 2,400 responding parents said it was suitable.

breakdown.analysis: Who visits a show's fan website? Fans. Asking them is like polling people at a pizza place about whether pizza is good. The sample is tilted toward the answer. Prephrase: the sample isn't representative of parents nationwide.

choices.note: Possible, but it's not the main problem. Even if every respondent had young kids, they're still fans of the show.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We polled adults about a kids' show without checking whether any of them have kids.

choices.note: CORRECT. Parents on the show's fan site are likely to like the show more than parents in general. The conclusion about all parents rests on a biased sample.
The conclusion is about proportions ('vast majority'), and so is the evidence (91 percent). No percent-versus-number confusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: 91 percent of respondents approved, so millions of parents approve.

choices.note: The argument doesn't accuse anyone of deliberate deception. It just uses a bad sample.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The network clearly rigged the poll, so its results are false.

choices.note: Trap. 2,400 is a decent size. The problem isn't how many but who.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Twelve parents at a playground liked the show, so most parents nationwide do.

questions.stimulus: In September, a transportation researcher interviewed 500 people locking bicycles at racks in downtown Halvern on weekday mornings. Seventy percent of them said that they cycle to work at least three days a week throughout the winter. From these interviews the researcher concluded that most of Halvern's bicycle commuters continue to cycle to work regularly during the winter months, and that the city's winter maintenance of bicycle lanes is well used.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Most of the people interviewed had lived in Halvern for more than five years at the time of the interviews.
The city clears snow from downtown bicycle lanes far more promptly than it clears lanes in outlying neighborhoods.
Some of the people locking bicycles at the downtown racks declined to answer the researcher's questions.
People who cycle to downtown jobs are typical of Halvern's bicycle commuters in how often they cycle in winter.
In several cities comparable to Halvern, most bicycle commuters stop cycling to work once winter begins.
questions.explanation: Sampling: the researcher generalizes from cyclists at downtown racks to all of Halvern's bicycle commuters. D strengthens the argument by establishing that the downtown group is representative on exactly the trait being measured. B is the tempting trap, but it points the wrong way: if downtown lanes are cleared sooner, downtown cyclists may ride in winter more than other commuters do, which weakens the generalization. E also weakens, and A is irrelevant to representativeness.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most of Halvern's bicycle commuters keep cycling regularly in winter, and the city's winter lane maintenance is well used.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70% of 500 people locking bikes at downtown racks on weekday mornings in September said they cycle to work at least three days a week all winter.

breakdown.analysis: The sample is downtown cyclists. The conclusion is about all of Halvern's bike commuters. Downtown riders might be different: shorter rides, better-cleared lanes. It's like surveying gym-goers at 6 a.m. and concluding most members are early risers. To strengthen, show the downtown group is typical on the thing being measured: winter cycling.

choices.note: How long they've lived there doesn't make them representative of commuters' winter habits. Irrelevant.
Trap. If downtown lanes are cleared faster, downtown cyclists may ride in winter more than others. That makes the sample less representative and weakens the argument.
Some people declining to answer opens the door to a non-response bias. If anything, it slightly weakens.
CORRECT. If downtown commuters are typical of all Halvern commuters in winter cycling, then the sample speaks for the whole group. That closes the gap.
This suggests winter cycling usually drops off, which weakens the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Northline, a regional airline, wanted to know whether its passengers would pay an extra fee for assigned seating. It surveyed passengers on its Friday-evening flights between Corvale and the capital, flights used mostly by business travelers whose employers reimburse their fares. Eighty percent of the respondents said they would pay the fee. Northline concluded that most of its passengers would be willing to pay extra for assigned seating.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: To estimate how many county residents own fishing gear, a researcher interviewed shoppers at the county's largest sporting-goods store on the opening weekend of trout season. Most owned gear, so most residents do.

A library drew 1,000 names at random from its complete list of cardholders and asked each whether they had borrowed an e-book. Sixty percent had, so probably most of its cardholders have borrowed an e-book at least once.
A survey of members of the Tarrow Cycling Club found that they report fewer sick days than other adults do. So cycling regularly must be what keeps the club's members from falling ill as often.

The share of complaints the Linden Clinic received about waiting times fell this year. So fewer of the clinic's patients were dissatisfied with waiting times this year than were dissatisfied last year.
Every player on the Granby hockey team is among the most skilled in the league. So the Granby team as a whole must be among the most skilled teams in the league.
questions.explanation: Northline generalizes to all its passengers from a subgroup chosen in a way that tilts it toward the answer (business travelers whose fares are reimbursed). A does the same: shoppers at a sporting-goods store on opening weekend are far likelier than residents generally to own fishing gear. B is the most tempting trap because it also generalizes from a survey, but its random sample from the full list is representative, so its reasoning is sound. C uses a survey but commits a causal flaw, D confuses a share of complaints with the number of dissatisfied patients, and E reasons from parts to the whole.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Northline passengers would pay extra for assigned seating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 80% of respondents on Friday-evening Corvale-capital flights, mostly business travelers whose fares are reimbursed, said they'd pay.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Survey a subgroup that's especially likely to say yes; most say yes; so most of the whole population would say yes.

breakdown.analysis: Business travelers whose employers pay their fares are the people least bothered by extra fees. They don't represent the vacationer counting pennies. It's like polling a steakhouse's diners on whether people like steak. Find the answer that generalizes from a subgroup tilted toward the result.

choices.note: CORRECT. Shoppers at a sporting-goods store on trout-season opening weekend are far more likely to own fishing gear than residents generally. Same biased sample, same overgeneralization.
Trap. Also a survey generalization, but the sample is random from the complete list. That's representative, so the reasoning is fine.
Different flaw: a causal leap. Club members feel healthier, so cycling must be the cause.
Different flaw: confuses a share of complaints with the number of dissatisfied patients.
Different flaw: part to whole. Skilled players don't guarantee a skilled team.

questions.stimulus: The Morrow Historical Society holds about 40,000 photographic prints made between 1880 and 1920. To assess their condition, the conservator Ines Faber examined the 400 prints that researchers had requested most often over the past decade and found that only 5 percent of them showed significant fading. Faber concluded that the collection as a whole is in good condition, and that the costly preservation program some board members have proposed is therefore unnecessary.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Frequent handling by researchers tends to accelerate the deterioration of photographic prints made during this period.
In comparable collections of prints from the same period, about 5 percent typically show significant fading.
Faber has argued on several previous occasions that the society spends too much on conservation.
Prints made between 1880 and 1920 are generally less prone to fading than prints made after 1950.
Prints often requested by researchers are kept in climate-controlled cabinets; the rest are stored in an unheated attic.
questions.explanation: Sampling: Faber generalizes from the 400 most-requested prints to the whole collection. E shows that this subgroup was stored under far better conditions than the rest, so its low rate of fading probably understates the damage elsewhere. A is the most tempting trap, but it points the wrong way: if handling accelerates deterioration, the sampled prints should be in worse shape than average, which makes Faber's finding more reassuring. C attacks Faber's motives rather than her reasoning, and B and D, if anything, support her.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The collection as a whole is in good condition, so the costly preservation program is unnecessary.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Faber examined the 400 most-requested prints out of 40,000; only 5 percent showed significant fading.

breakdown.analysis: Faber checked 1 percent of the collection, and not a random 1 percent: the most-requested prints. Those might be treated very differently from the rest. It's like judging a library's condition by the books on the front display. To weaken, show the sampled prints aren't representative, especially in a way that makes them look better than the rest.

choices.note: Trap, and it points the wrong way. If handling speeds up deterioration, the most-handled prints should be in worse shape than average. Their good condition would then be extra reassuring.
This says 5 percent fading is normal for such collections, which, if anything, supports Faber's 'good condition' verdict.
This attacks Faber's motives, not her reasoning. Her sample could still be fine.
Comparing with post-1950 prints doesn't touch whether her sample represents this collection. If anything, it supports her.

CORRECT. The sampled prints live in climate-controlled cabinets; the rest sit in an unheated attic. The sample is in much better conditions than the bulk of the collection, so its low fading rate likely understates the damage.

questions.stimulus: A study of the Ferrin County small-claims court examined every case filed over three years in which a plaintiff who had initially hired a lawyer later chose to proceed without one. Those plaintiffs won 72 percent of their cases, slightly more than the 68 percent won by plaintiffs who kept their lawyers throughout. The study's authors concluded that small-claims plaintiffs generally fare at least as well without lawyers as with them, and that the county's program subsidizing lawyers for such plaintiffs should be ended.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses the rate at which plaintiffs won their cases with the number of cases plaintiffs won
presupposes that the subsidy program is the only means by which plaintiffs could obtain legal help
generalizes from a self-selected group whose reason for selecting itself may also affect the outcome measured
treats the absence of evidence that lawyers help such plaintiffs as evidence that lawyers do not help them
recommends ending a program solely on the grounds that the program costs the county more than it is worth
questions.explanation: Sampling, through self-selection: plaintiffs who dropped their lawyers probably did so because they judged their cases strong, and case strength also drives win rates, so this group tells us little about plaintiffs in general. C describes this abstractly. D is the most tempting trap because it names a real flaw, but the authors rely on positive evidence (a comparison of win rates), not on a mere lack of evidence. A is wrong because the argument reasons entirely from rates, and E attributes to the argument a cost rationale it never offers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Small-claims plaintiffs generally fare at least as well without lawyers, and the lawyer-subsidy program should end.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Plaintiffs who dropped their lawyers won 72% of cases; plaintiffs who kept lawyers won 68%.

breakdown.analysis: Who drops a lawyer mid-case? Probably people who think their case is a slam dunk. Strong cases win more. So this group isn't typical, and the reason they chose to go solo also explains why they won. It's like noting that students who skip review sessions score well, when the ones who skip are the ones who already know the material. Prephrase: a self-selected group used to generalize.

choices.note: The argument reasons only from rates (72% vs. 68%) and concludes about how plaintiffs fare. No rate-versus-number mix-up.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Plaintiffs without lawyers won 72% of their cases, so they won more cases than plaintiffs with lawyers.

choices.note: The argument doesn't assume the subsidy is the only source of legal help. It argues lawyers don't help much.
choices.example: Example of flaw: If we end the subsidy, no plaintiff will ever get a lawyer again.

choices.note: CORRECT. Plaintiffs chose to drop their lawyers, likely because their cases looked strong, and case strength also drives win rates. Generalizing from that group to all plaintiffs is the flaw.
Trap. The authors use positive evidence, a comparison of win rates. They don't argue from a mere lack of evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No study has shown lawyers help small-claims plaintiffs, so they don't.

choices.note: The argument never talks about cost-benefit or what the program costs the county.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The subsidy costs $2 million a year, which is more than it's worth, so end it.

questions.stimulus: Councilor Brandt: Ostrava Falls requires every resident who drives a car to register it with the city and display a registration sticker. Bicycles, like cars, are vehicles that share the city's streets, and riders of bicycles, like drivers of cars, must obey the city's traffic signals. So, to be consistent, the city should likewise require every resident who commutes by bicycle to register the bicycle with the city and display a sticker.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that many residents who commute by bicycle to work also own and regularly drive cars
takes for granted that every bicycle commuter would comply with a registration requirement
presumes without justification that most residents of Ostrava Falls drive cars
relies on similarities between cars and bicycles without showing they are alike in respects that justify registration
assumes that whatever rule the city legally requires of its residents is also something they are morally obligated to do
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: Brandt notes that bicycles and cars both use streets and obey signals, but never shows that these shared features are the reasons cars must be registered (rather than, say, their speed, mass, or taxation). D identifies this. A is the tempting trap, but whether bicycle commuters also drive has no bearing on whether the comparison supports registering bicycles. B and C describe assumptions the argument does not need, and E introduces a moral claim it never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should require bicycle commuters to register their bikes and display a sticker.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cars must be registered; bicycles, like cars, are vehicles sharing the streets; cyclists, like drivers, must obey traffic signals.

breakdown.analysis: Cars and bikes are alike in some ways. But are those the reasons cars get registered? Cars are registered because they're heavy, fast, taxed, and cause serious harm. Sharing the street and obeying lights aren't obviously why. By this logic, pedestrians share the streets and obey signals too, so they should wear registration stickers. Prephrase: the analogy relies on similarities that don't justify the rule.

choices.note: Trap. Whether cyclists also drive cars has nothing to do with whether the cars-bikes comparison justifies registering bikes.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Bike commuters already register their cars, so registering bikes would be redundant, and the argument ignores this.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need everyone to comply. A rule can be justified even if some people break it.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We should require bike registration because every cyclist will happily follow the rule.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need most residents to drive. It's about consistency of treatment, not numbers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Most residents drive, so the city's rules should be written around drivers.

choices.note: CORRECT. Brandt points to shared features (using streets, obeying signals) without showing those are the features that justify registering cars.
The argument is about consistency in the city's rules. It never brings in moral obligation.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The law requires registration, so registering your car is a moral duty.

questions.stimulus: The coastal town of Merrin is considering building a reverse-osmosis desalination plant. Supporters point to Sallow Cove, a town about 300 kilometers to the south, which built a similar plant ten years ago and has since enjoyed a reliable supply of drinking water at a price its residents consider reasonable. Because Merrin and Sallow Cove are similar in population and both draw their seawater from the same ocean, supporters conclude that a plant in Merrin would likewise provide reliable water at a reasonable cost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: The engineering firm that designed and built the Sallow Cove plant has since gone out of business entirely.
Residents of Sallow Cove now pay considerably more for their water than they did before their desalination plant was built.
Merrin's population is expected to grow slightly faster than Sallow Cove's over the next decade.
Several other towns along the same coast have built desalination plants that supply their residents with water reliably.
Seawater off Merrin holds far more silt than that off Sallow Cove, and silt sharply raises the cost of running reverse-osmosis plants.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the supporters rest their prediction on similarities between the two towns. E reveals a difference in exactly the respect that matters to a desalination plant's cost and reliability, the quality of the intake water, so Sallow Cove's success is a poor guide for Merrin. B is the tempting trap, but paying more than before is compatible with residents still finding the price reasonable, which is all the premise claims. C names a difference too slight to matter, and D supports the supporters' view.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A desalination plant in Merrin would provide reliable water at a reasonable cost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sallow Cove's similar plant has done so for ten years; the towns have similar populations and draw seawater from the same ocean.

breakdown.analysis: An analogy is only as good as its similarities. Same ocean and same population size are pretty thin. What matters for a desalination plant is things like water quality and energy costs. It's like assuming your new car will get the same mileage as your neighbor's because you both live on the same street. To weaken, find a difference in a respect that matters to cost or reliability.

choices.note: The firm going out of business doesn't show Merrin's plant would fail. Merrin could hire a different firm, and Sallow Cove's plant still works.
Trap. Paying more than before is compatible with the price still being reasonable, which is all the premise claims.
A slightly faster growth rate is too small a difference to undermine the comparison.
More towns with reliable plants supports the supporters' view.
CORRECT. Merrin's seawater has far more silt, and silt sharply raises operating costs. That's a difference in exactly the respect that matters, so Sallow Cove's success is a poor guide.

questions.stimulus: Breeding queens for gentleness has succeeded in the apiaries of the Varn Islands, where nearly every colony is now docile. Our mainland apiaries keep the same species of honeybee as the islands' apiaries, house their colonies in the same design of hive, and feed them the same supplemental syrup in winter. So if we adopt the islands' breeding program, our colonies will become docile as well.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Since the Eastvale apiaries switched to a new winter feed, their honey yields have risen every year. So the new winter feed must be responsible for the higher honey yields in the Eastvale apiaries.

A tutoring method raised reading scores at Elmhurst School. Brookside uses the same reading textbooks and has classrooms of the same size as Elmhurst's. So the method will raise reading scores at Brookside too.

A drainage design prevented flooding on Route 9. Route 12 matches Route 9 in soil, slope, and rainfall, the factors that determine whether such a design works. So the design will prevent flooding on Route 12 too.
Each structural component of the Tarn footbridge passed its load test. So the Tarn footbridge as a whole would pass a load test, since it is made up entirely of components that have passed.
The twelve beekeepers who answered the cooperative's newsletter survey all favor the new labeling rules. So the cooperative's beekeepers in general must favor the new labeling rules.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the argument predicts that a program will work in a second setting because that setting shares features (species, hive design, feed) never shown to be what made the program work. B has the same structure: shared textbooks and classroom size are not shown to explain why tutoring succeeded. C is the most tempting trap, but its argument says outright that the shared features determine whether the design works, so its analogy is sound. A shares the subject matter but commits a causal flaw, D reasons from parts to the whole, and E generalizes from a self-selected sample.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If we adopt the islands' breeding program, our colonies will become docile too.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The program worked in the Varn Islands; mainland apiaries keep the same species, use the same hive design, and feed the same syrup.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Program worked in place A; place B shares features not shown to be why it worked; so it will work in B.

breakdown.analysis: Same species, hives, and syrup. But are those why the breeding worked? Maybe the islands' isolation kept wild, aggressive drones from mating with the queens. On the mainland, that might not hold. It's like assuming a diet that worked for your friend will work for you because you both wear the same shoe size. Find the answer that transfers a result on similarities never shown to matter.

choices.note: Different flaw: a causal leap from sequence. Yields rose after the feed change, so the feed caused it. Same beekeeping subject, different structure.

CORRECT. Same textbooks and class size are offered as the basis for predicting the tutoring method will work at Brookside, without showing those features are why it worked at Elmhurst. Same flawed analogy.
Trap. This one says outright that soil, slope, and rainfall are the factors that determine whether the design works. So the analogy is sound, not flawed.
Different flaw: part to whole. Components passing doesn't guarantee the whole bridge passes.
Different flaw: generalizing from a small, self-selected sample of survey respondents.

questions.stimulus: Educational psychologists found that preschoolers who played the board game Number Trail for twenty minutes a day markedly improved their counting skills within a month. The producers of the children's television program Count with Kip have adapted the game's puzzles into on-screen segments, in which the host works through each puzzle step by step. Therefore, preschoolers who watch twenty minutes of Count with Kip a day should improve their counting skills just as markedly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: More preschoolers watch Count with Kip each day than play Number Trail.
Preschoolers who watch Count with Kip will enjoy the program as much as the children in the study enjoyed Number Trail.
The benefit of Number Trail did not depend mainly on children moving pieces and counting aloud themselves.
Count with Kip's segments reproduce the puzzles of Number Trail without any alteration to their content.
The preschoolers in the psychologists' study came from a broad range of economic backgrounds.
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the argument assumes that watching puzzles worked on screen is relevantly like playing them. Negate C: if the gains came mainly from children handling the pieces and counting aloud themselves, which viewers do not do, then the analogy fails and the conclusion loses its support. D is the most tempting trap, but it is too strong; minor changes to the puzzles would not undermine the argument. E raises a sampling concern the argument does not depend on, and A and B are not required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Preschoolers who watch twenty minutes of Count with Kip daily should improve their counting just as markedly.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Preschoolers who played Number Trail twenty minutes a day markedly improved; the show adapts the game's puzzles, with the host working through each one.

breakdown.analysis: Playing a game and watching someone else play it aren't the same. If the gains came from kids moving pieces and counting out loud themselves, watching won't deliver them. It's like assuming you'll get fit watching workout videos because they show the same exercises. So the argument must assume the benefit didn't come mainly from the hands-on part.

choices.note: How many kids watch versus play doesn't affect whether watching works as well. Negating it does nothing.
choices.negation: At least as many preschoolers play Number Trail each day as watch Count with Kip.

choices.note: Not required. Kids might enjoy it less and still improve. Negating it gives only a vague worry, not a collapse.
choices.negation: Preschoolers who watch Count with Kip will not enjoy it as much as the study's children enjoyed Number Trail.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the benefit depended mainly on kids moving pieces and counting aloud themselves. Viewers don't do that, so the analogy breaks and the conclusion loses its support.
choices.negation: The benefit of Number Trail depended mainly on children moving pieces and counting aloud themselves.

choices.note: Trap. Too strong. Small changes to the puzzles wouldn't sink the argument. Negate it (some minor alteration) and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Count with Kip's segments alter the content of at least some Number Trail puzzles in some way.

choices.note: A sampling worry the argument doesn't depend on. Negate it (narrow range of backgrounds) and the argument is weakened a little at most, not destroyed.
choices.negation: The preschoolers in the study did not come from a broad range of economic backgrounds.

questions.stimulus: Lichenologist: Critics of our plan to move the lichen communities on the Brannock quarry walls to the protected Tolley cliffs before the quarry is blasted say that such transplants usually fail. Admittedly, relocated lichens often die. But mosses that were moved from this same quarry to the Tolley cliffs five years ago are thriving today. Mosses, like lichens, lack true roots and absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain. So the lichens, too, will thrive on the Tolley cliffs.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: infers that one kind of organism will fare as another did because of a shared trait, without showing that the trait explains the other's success
attacks the critics' motives for opposing the relocation plan rather than responding to the evidence on which their objection is actually based
applies to each individual lichen community on the quarry walls a generalization that holds only for relocated lichens taken as a group
concludes that an outcome will occur merely because no one has shown that the outcome is impossible under the circumstances
overlooks the possibility that the lichen communities could survive in the quarry even after the blasting has taken place
questions.explanation: Flawed analogy: the lichenologist concedes that relocated lichens often die, then relies on the success of mosses, citing only that both lack roots. She never shows that lacking roots is why the mosses thrived, and lichens may differ in other relevant ways. A states this abstractly. D is the most tempting trap because it names a real flaw, but the argument rests on positive evidence (the mosses' success), not on a lack of disproof. C describes a part-whole error the argument does not make, and B and E describe moves it never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The relocated lichens will thrive on the Tolley cliffs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Admittedly, relocated lichens often die; but mosses moved from the same quarry to Tolley five years ago are thriving; mosses, like lichens, lack true roots and absorb water and nutrients from air and rain.

breakdown.analysis: The lichenologist leans on one shared trait: no roots. But is that why the mosses thrived? Maybe mosses tolerate disturbance better, grow faster, or need different rock. Lichens are a fungus-alga partnership and famously sensitive. It's like predicting your cat will love the new apartment because your goldfish did, since neither likes loud noises. Prephrase: an analogy built on a trait not shown to matter.

choices.note: CORRECT. Lichens are predicted to fare like mosses because both lack roots, but the argument never shows rootlessness is why the mosses thrived.
No attack on motives. She concedes the critics' point and responds with evidence about mosses.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics just want the quarry blasting delayed, so we can ignore their concerns about transplants.

choices.note: No part-whole move. The argument doesn't apply a group statistic to individual communities.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Relocated lichens as a group usually die, so this particular lichen community will certainly die.

choices.note: Trap. The argument has positive evidence: the mosses' success. It doesn't argue from a lack of disproof.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Nobody has shown the lichens can't survive at Tolley, so they will thrive there.

choices.note: The argument never considers leaving the lichens in the quarry, and the plan assumes the quarry will be blasted. This isn't where the reasoning goes wrong.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lichens must be moved, because there's no chance they'd survive the blasting (ignoring evidence they might).

questions.stimulus: Last spring, Skyhop, a regional airline, replaced the aging turboprops on its Dunmore-Kessel route with new regional jets. Since then, the share of flights on that route arriving on time has risen from 71 percent to 88 percent, and passenger complaints about the route have fallen by half. Both improvements are due to the new jets' greater speed and mechanical reliability. Clearly, then, the new jets were the best choice Skyhop could have made for the Dunmore-Kessel route.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses a percentage-point increase in on-time arrivals with an increase in the absolute number of on-time flights
presumes without justification that the new jets, rather than some other factor, caused the improvements on the route
relies on complaints from passengers who may not be representative of everyone who flies the route
assumes that what was true of the Dunmore-Kessel route must also be true of every other route Skyhop flies
infers that an option was the best one available merely from evidence that it produced improvements
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the evidence shows the jets were an improvement over the old turboprops, but the conclusion claims they were the best of all possible choices, though other options might have done even better. E identifies this. B is the tempting trap, but the stimulus states as a premise that the improvements are due to the jets, so the argument does not presume causation without support. D misdescribes a conclusion that is limited to one route.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new jets were the best choice Skyhop could have made for the route.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the switch, on-time arrivals rose from 71% to 88% and complaints fell by half; both improvements are due to the jets' speed and reliability.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence shows the jets were better than the old turboprops. The conclusion says they were the best possible choice. Those aren't the same. Maybe newer turboprops, or a different jet, would have done even better. It's like saying your new phone is the best phone on the market because it beats your old one. Prephrase: 'improvement' slides into 'best.'

choices.note: The argument reasons from the percentage of on-time flights and never claims anything about absolute numbers.
choices.example: Example of flaw: On-time arrivals went from 71% to 88%, so many more flights must be running on time overall.

choices.note: Trap. The stimulus states as a premise that the improvements are due to the jets. You accept premises as true, so causation isn't the weak spot.
choices.example: Example of flaw: On-time rates rose after the jets arrived, so the jets must be responsible.

choices.note: Complaints are just one piece of evidence, and the argument doesn't rely on them being representative. The flaw is the jump to 'best.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: The few passengers who wrote in loved the jets, so all passengers do.

choices.note: The conclusion is limited to the Dunmore-Kessel route. No generalization to other routes.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The jets improved the Dunmore-Kessel route, so they'd improve every Skyhop route.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence shows the jets produced improvements. The conclusion says they were the best option available. Other options might have done even better.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, the Delmar County small-claims court began requiring the parties in every dispute to attend a mediation session before any trial. Since then, the average time from filing to resolution has dropped from five months to seven weeks, a drop that an independent audit attributed entirely to the mediation requirement. Court administrators therefore conclude that the mediation requirement has made the court better at serving the people who bring their disputes to it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Most people who bring disputes to the court prefer resolving them through mediation rather than at trial.
The mediation requirement did not lengthen the time needed to resolve the cases that still went to trial afterward.
Any decline in the fairness of outcomes since mediation began is not great enough to outweigh faster resolution.
No other small-claims court in the region has achieved a comparable reduction in time to resolution.
Mediation sessions cost the court considerably less to administer than full trials before a magistrate do.
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the evidence concerns only speed, but the conclusion claims the court now serves people better overall. Negate C: if outcomes became so much less fair that this outweighs the gain in speed, the court is not serving people better, and the argument fails. B is the tempting trap, but the average already fell sharply, so the argument does not need trial-bound cases to be unaffected. A is too strong, and D and E are irrelevant to whether the people served are better off.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The mediation requirement has made the court better at serving people who bring disputes to it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Time to resolution dropped from five months to seven weeks; an independent audit attributed the drop entirely to mediation.

breakdown.analysis: The evidence is about speed. The conclusion is about serving people better overall. Faster isn't automatically better: a fast-food meal is quick, but that doesn't make it a better meal. If mediation pressured people into unfair settlements, the court could be faster and worse. So the argument must assume any loss of fairness isn't big enough to outweigh the speed gain.

choices.note: Too strong. The court can serve people better even if most would prefer a trial. Negating it doesn't collapse the argument.
choices.negation: At least half of the people who bring disputes to the court do not prefer mediation to trial.

choices.note: Trap. The average already dropped sharply, and that's what the argument relies on. Even if trial cases got a bit slower, the overall speed gain holds. Negating it doesn't sink the argument.
choices.negation: The mediation requirement lengthened the time needed to resolve cases that still went to trial.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: outcomes got so much less fair that it outweighs the faster resolution. Then the court isn't serving people better, and the conclusion fails.
choices.negation: A decline in the fairness of outcomes since mediation began is great enough to outweigh faster resolution.

choices.note: What other courts achieved doesn't matter. The conclusion is about whether this court got better. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: At least one other small-claims court in the region has achieved a comparable reduction in time to resolution.

choices.note: Cost to the court isn't the same as service to the people. Negating it doesn't affect the conclusion.
choices.negation: Mediation sessions do not cost the court considerably less to administer than full trials.

questions.stimulus: Digitizing the Lantry Archive's collection of glass-plate negatives would make thousands of historically important images available to researchers anywhere in the world, many of whom cannot travel to the archive. Moreover, a digital copy would preserve each image even if the fragile original plate were later broken. Hence, digitizing the negatives is the best use the archive could make of this year's limited conservation budget.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: A frost-resistant pear variety would survive Orlen Valley winters better than the cooperative's current variety, and it ripens earlier. So replanting with it is the wisest investment the cooperative could make this decade.

Digitizing the Pell Archive's maps would help researchers, and researchers are the archive's principal users. So digitizing the maps would help the archive's principal users, whatever else it might accomplish.

When the Corrin Museum digitized its photographs, visits to its website tripled. The Dunley Museum is about the same size as the Corrin Museum, so digitizing its photographs will triple visits to its website too.
Any archive that receives a Halsey grant must have a fireproof vault. The Tamsin Archive has just installed a fireproof vault. So the Tamsin Archive will receive a Halsey grant this year.
No one has shown that the Vell Library's rare-book room is at risk of flooding. So spending money to protect that room from flooding would be a waste of the library's limited resources.
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the argument cites benefits of digitizing and concludes that digitizing is the best use of the budget, ignoring alternatives that might be better still. A shifts the same way, from a variety's advantages to the claim that it is the wisest possible investment. B is the most tempting trap because it shares the subject, but its conclusion follows validly from its premises. C relies on a flawed analogy, D confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one, and E treats an absence of evidence as proof.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Digitizing the negatives is the best use of this year's limited conservation budget.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Digitizing would make thousands of images available worldwide and would preserve each image even if the original plate broke.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Option X has benefits; so X is the best possible use of limited resources.

breakdown.analysis: Listing benefits shows digitizing is a good idea. It doesn't show it's the best idea. Maybe the plates are cracking right now and stabilizing them is more urgent. It's like saying a gym membership is the best possible use of your money because exercise is healthy. Find the answer that goes from 'has advantages' to 'the best option there is.'

choices.note: CORRECT. The pear variety has advantages (frost resistance, earlier ripening), and the argument concludes it's the wisest investment possible. Same jump from benefits to best.
Trap: same subject matter, but the conclusion (it would help the principal users) follows directly from the premises. Valid, not flawed.
Different flaw: a weak analogy based on museum size.
Different flaw: a necessary condition (fireproof vault) treated as sufficient for getting the grant.
Different flaw: absence of evidence of risk treated as proof there's no risk.

questions.stimulus: In a year-long study, four-year-olds who were randomly assigned to watch the program Wordling Way for half an hour each weekday learned significantly more new vocabulary words than comparable children assigned to watch other programs. Because random assignment ruled out pre-existing differences between the groups, the program's producers concluded that watching Wordling Way improves the overall language development of young children.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Some children in both groups of the study also watched other educational programs at home on weekends during the study.
Vocabulary gains in young children are not reliably accompanied by gains in sentence construction, comprehension, or other aspects of language.
The words taught on Wordling Way are drawn from the vocabulary lists used in many kindergarten curricula across the country.
The study of Wordling Way was funded by the program's own producers, who stood to profit from any favorable results the study produced.
Most of the children assigned to watch Wordling Way said that they liked it better than the other programs they watched at home.
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the study measured only vocabulary, but the producers conclude that the program improves overall language development. B weakens the argument by showing that vocabulary gains are not a reliable sign of gains in the other components of language development. D is the most tempting trap, but it only questions the source; given random assignment, it gives no reason to doubt the study's finding or to think the inference from vocabulary to overall development is any weaker. A affects both groups alike, and C and E are irrelevant to the gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Watching Wordling Way improves young children's overall language development.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a randomized year-long study, children assigned to watch it learned significantly more new vocabulary than comparable children watching other programs.

breakdown.analysis: The study measured vocabulary. The conclusion is about overall language development: grammar, comprehension, and so on. Vocabulary is one slice. It's like proving a drill makes kids better at free throws and concluding it makes them better basketball players. The randomization handles cause; the gap is scope. To weaken, show vocabulary gains don't track overall language gains.

choices.note: This affects both groups equally, so random assignment still holds. It doesn't weaken the comparison.
CORRECT. If vocabulary gains don't reliably come with gains in sentence construction or comprehension, then the vocabulary result says little about overall language development.
Where the words come from doesn't touch whether vocabulary gains reflect overall language development. Irrelevant.
Trap. It questions the source, but with random assignment there's no specific reason to doubt the finding. And it doesn't affect the leap from vocabulary to overall development.
Kids liking the show doesn't bear on whether vocabulary gains mean overall language gains.

questions.stimulus: Desalination engineer: Critics claim that the Rennet Bay plant uses too much energy to be sustainable. Yet in each of its first three years of operation, the plant used less energy per liter of fresh water produced than the regional average for water treatment facilities of every kind. Granted, those three years brought unusually warm seawater, and warm water reduces the energy that reverse osmosis requires. Still, the record speaks for itself: the plant's energy use per liter will remain below that regional average throughout its planned forty-year life.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: rests on a comparison between the plant and facilities that treat water by different methods and from different sources
attacks the critics' motives for questioning the plant's sustainability instead of addressing the evidence for their claim
confuses the plant's energy use per liter of fresh water with the total amount of energy the plant uses each year
projects onto an entire future period a pattern observed under conditions it acknowledges to be atypical
treats the absence of evidence that the plant is unsustainable as proof that the plant is sustainable
questions.explanation: Scope shift: the engineer extends a three-year record to a forty-year forecast, even after conceding that those three years had unusually warm seawater, which lowers energy needs. D describes this abstractly. E is the most tempting trap because it names a familiar flaw, but the engineer cites positive evidence (measured energy use), not a mere lack of evidence. A is wrong because the conclusion is itself a comparison with the regional average, so using that benchmark is not a flaw, and C invents a confusion the argument, which reasons only about per-liter use, never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Rennet Bay plant's energy use per liter will stay below the regional average for its whole forty-year life.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In each of its first three years, it used less energy per liter than the regional average; granted, those years had unusually warm seawater, which lowers energy needs.

breakdown.analysis: Three good years, and the engineer admits they were unusual: warm water makes reverse osmosis cheaper. Then she projects forty years of the same. It's like a rookie having three seasons with a strong tailwind and you predicting a forty-year record. Prephrase: projecting atypical conditions onto the whole future.

choices.note: The conclusion itself is a comparison with the regional average, so using that benchmark is fine. Not the flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our plant uses less energy than a typical household boiler, so it's efficient compared to other desalination plants.

choices.note: The engineer doesn't mention the critics' motives at all.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Critics of the plant just want to sell their own technology, so their sustainability claims can be ignored.

choices.note: The argument reasons only about per-liter use, start to finish. No confusion with total energy.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The plant uses little energy per liter, so it must use little energy overall.

choices.note: CORRECT. A three-year record from unusually warm years, which she admits lower energy needs, is projected onto all forty years.
Trap. The engineer cites positive evidence: measured energy use. She isn't arguing from a lack of evidence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the plant is unsustainable, so it is sustainable.
